explanation: No clear shared feature: strongest on ' WITHOUT' in the Apache 'AS IS' BASIS, WITHOUT WARRANTIES license line, but also fires on assorted function words, sentence-ending periods and commas in marketing/explanatory prose and odd code tokens. Outside the license phrase, activation is hard to predict.

Fires on middle subword pieces of rare or foreign proper nouns and technical words that are split into several tokens (e.g. Dj-urg-ården, BRE-CK-enridge, Mie-cz-ysław, Ud-var-Hazy, r-ink, cr-ani-ectomy, E-CG). Unusual consonant clusters like 'cz', 'CK', 'CG' fire most. Whole common words do not fire.

Fires on tokens of technical/scientific compound terms, mostly anatomical or astronomical prefix-word pieces (intr-ac-ranial, intr-al-obar, gal-actic, Milky Way, subd-ural) and statistical terms (confidence interval, pooled sensitivity, sensitivity analysis, background noise). The top hit is a GIS term (Raster-ize). Ordinary prose is weak.

Fires on verbs meaning to perform or carry out an activity: 'conduct' (to conduct a study/review/operations), 'out' in 'carry/carried/carrying out', and 'perform'. It also fires on the 'conduct' root in conducting/conductive/superconductivity. Weaker on other generic action verbs such as run, done and carries.

Fires on tokens in political, military and sports-contest news: voting (vote, voted), fighting/fight against ISIS, leaders' names (Vladimir Putin, Omar al-, SPD), conceded defeat, ruling party, and match scores (3-2, 6-5). Unrelated hits include a version-number period in a jquery URL.

Fires on a short subword fragment near the start of a word that has been split into pieces, usually its first or second piece: se-psis, Eins-ch-üchterungen, enf-antillages, un-tr-oubled, my-oc-lonic, ' f'-oment, ' g'-annets, ' def'-rauding, an-est-hetics. This holds across languages and is driven by tokenization rather than meaning. Whole-word tokens are weak.

Mixture: fires on modal or future auxiliaries after a subject (will/would/can/may/could, e.g. 'Any help will be', 'Any answer would be appreciated', 'it will be useful'). It also fires on middle subword pieces of foreign personal and religious names (Bartol-ome-o, Bh-ag-avatha, Naz-are-ne, Madhub-ala) and on HTML meta charset punctuation.

Fires on the letter sequence 'ir'/'Ir'/'IR' as a subword token, in names (Irwin, Irina, Irfaan, Qirko, Thir-), words (expiratory, encircling, memoir, Irresistible, Hepadnaviridae) and code identifiers (FLIR). It also fires on similar r-final pieces such as 'Pir', 'ar', 'R', 'Cir' and 'Dir'.

Mainly fires on ' import' in Python 'from X.Y import Z' statements and on code-template openers like '<?php' and '<%='. Long runs of zeros fire maximally, and some CJK characters and other code tokens also fire. Most of it is code syntax tokens.

Fires on a word within a verb or adjective phrase that sets up a continuation, such as 'could' (we could face, Operation could not), 'next' (the next step/chapter/generation), 'be' (blessed to be), and deciding, carries, runs, continue. The examples are diverse and only loosely united.

Fires on tokens inside formatting or markup structures: citation markers and numbers inside ^[@bib2]^ or [@CR1], percent and unit punctuation in statistics ('15.7 l min-1/%', '(5%)'), and identifiers inside code or templates ($Revision$, __MODULE__, assembly registers, LaTeX \right). These are heterogeneous syntactic positions.

Fires on tokens in programming Q&A and code contexts, especially method or assertion names after a dot (t.equal, self.assertEqual, .shouldExecuteOk, Class.create), test directives (CHECK:), error-message words (No suitable driver, no known class) and tech names (GPIO, Selenium, DDL). It also fires somewhat on technical terms in scientific or medical prose (contractions, visual analogue, resolution).

Weak, scattered pattern: fires on tokens in narrative or news prose about events and transactions, such as before (being loaned), fear of, signed up / sign up / sign in, fell through, found, dropped out, and down payment. There is no clear token or context rule.

Fires on tokens in boilerplate or structural text: code operators (this == o, short *), DOI and citation periods, legal or license phrasing ('subject to the', 'On order of the Court', 'S.W.2d'), 'Sent from my', '// +build', and web navigation text. There is no single concept.
